title: Improve performance of path_rel
description:
`fs::path_rel` is suprisingly slow on large vectors. I use it regularly on the `FilePath` output of `read_csv(..., .id="FilePath")`, where most of the vector is severely duplicated (# of total rows >> # files). This is one of the reasons I developed the `deduped` package in the first place.

There are 3 simple opportunities for performance improvement:

1. Hoist `starts <- path_split(start)` out of the loop since start is guaranteed to be a single, fixed string.
2. Deduplicate the `paths` vector before the loop to reduce the number of R loop iterations (same strategy as `deduped` package but using base R)
3. Create internal version of `path_common` that takes the split pieces as arguments so that the splitting of all paths can be vectorized outside the R loop.

title: Feature Request: Allow dir_ls glob/regex patterns to ignore the supplied path
description:
`dir_ls` glob/regex patterns act on the whole path, including what was passed by `path`. Often this can be accidentally misleading since the folder path itself contains a pattern (maybe even accidentally) that breaks the intended logic. 

Request: it would be great if there were an argument to `dir_ls` to ignore the part of the path that was already supplied in `path` (effectively filtering only on the relative path).

Simple reprex:
``` r
temp <- tempfile("T Cell") |> fs::dir_create()

tryCatch({
   good_path <- fs::path(temp, "T Cell Data.csv")
   bad_path <-  fs::path(temp, "Other Data.csv")
   
   readr::write_csv(data.frame(), good_path)
   readr::write_csv(data.frame(), bad_path)
   
   ls_result <- fs::dir_ls(temp, glob="*T Cell*.csv")
   
   message("good_path found: ", good_path %in% ls_result)
   message("bad_path found: ", bad_path %in% ls_result)
},
finally = fs::dir_delete(temp) 
)
#> good_path found: TRUE
#> bad_path found: TRUE
```
<sup>Created on 2026-03-31 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>


Simple implementation extending current `dir_ls` with argument `filter_on_relative_path`.

```r
dir_ls <- function (path = ".", all = FALSE, recurse = FALSE, type = "any", 
    glob = NULL, regexp = NULL, invert = FALSE, fail = TRUE, filter_on_relative_path = FALSE,
    ..., recursive) 
{
    assert_no_missing(path)
    if (!missing(recursive)) {
        recurse <- recursive
        warning("`recursive` is deprecated, please use `recurse` instead", 
            immediate. = TRUE, call. = FALSE)
    }
    old <- path_expand(path)
    files <- as.character(dir_map(old, identity, all, recurse, 
        type, fail))

    # Simple case (same as existing)
    if (!filter_on_relative_path)
        return(path_filter(files, glob, regexp, invert = invert, ...))

   # Filter on relative path only.
   rel_files <- fs::path_rel(files, start=old)
   
   files[match(fs::path_filter(rel_files, glob, regexp, invert = invert, ...), rel_files)]
}

title: allow dir_ls to recursively list linked directories
description:
GIven this test, it looks like `dir_ls` intentionally does not follow symbolic links.

https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/81211aafd4cf968f942101e84ec6d835c1cb3e8a/tests/testthat/test-list.R#L23

I think it would be useful to list the contents of symbolically-linked directories.  Would you consider an option to support this?  For example, I'd like to see that the linked directory contains files A and B in the reprex below.


``` r
library(fs)

# modfied from example script at https://fs.r-lib.org/reference/copy.html

# make dir foo with multiple files
foo_dir <- dir_create(tempdir(), "foo")

file_create(foo_dir, c("A", "B"))

dir_ls(foo_dir)
#> /var/folders/wg/tq2qzp8s4yq1vhh2x_ldwc0c0000gn/T/Rtmp1Po6JD/foo/A
#> /var/folders/wg/tq2qzp8s4yq1vhh2x_ldwc0c0000gn/T/Rtmp1Po6JD/foo/B

# make dir bar with symbolic link to dir foo
bar_dir <- dir_create(tempdir(), "bar")
link_create(
  path = foo_dir,
  new_path = path(bar_dir, "loo")
)

# list bar contents
dir_ls(bar_dir, recurse = TRUE)
#> /var/folders/wg/tq2qzp8s4yq1vhh2x_ldwc0c0000gn/T/Rtmp1Po6JD/bar/loo
```

title: [BUG] `is_*()` return `FALSE` for nonexistent paths, but documentation says they should return `NA`
description:
`fs::is_*()` appears to behave inconsistently with its documentation, including `is_file()`, `is_dir()`, `is_link()` and `is_file_empty()`. My `fs` is the newest `2.1.0`.

The documentation for `is_file()` says:

```
A named logical vector, where the names give the paths. If the given object does not exist, `NA` is returned.
```

However, `is_file()` (and other funcs) returns `FALSE` for nonexistent paths instead of `NA`:

``` r
print(packageVersion("fs"))
#> [1] '2.1.0'

fs::is_file("unexisting_file.txt")
#> unexisting_file.txt 
#>               FALSE
fs::is_dir("unexisting_dir/")
#> unexisting_dir/ 
#>           FALSE
fs::is_link("unexisting_link")
#> unexisting_link 
#>           FALSE
fs::is_file_empty("unexisting_file.txt")
#> unexisting_file.txt 
#>               FALSE
```

There is the current R implementation code. Since `!is.na(res$type)` is used, nonexistent paths are converted to `FALSE` rather than propagating `NA`.

``` r
print(fs::is_file)
#> function (path, follow = TRUE) 
#> {
#>     res <- file_info(path, follow = follow)
#>     setNames(!is.na(res$type) & res$type == "file", path)
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x59ab3f485828>
#> <environment: namespace:fs>
```

This creates a mismatch between documentation and implementation. I wonder which behavior is intended:

- If `FALSE` is intended for nonexistent paths, the documentation should be updated.
- If `NA` is intended for nonexistent paths, the implementation should be changed.

I'm glad to create a PR to fix this.

title: vignette infelicity
description:
The vignette includes this
```r
do.call(rbind, lapply(list.files("path"), file.info))
```
However, this assumes the current working directory is `path`; moreover, `base::file.info` is already vectorized, so instead I'd recommend:
```r
file.info(list.files("path", full.names = TRUE))
```
Thank you for considering.

title: Compilation error on Windows ARM64 (R 4.5.3 / Rtools45): undeclared identifier 'EINVAL' in windows/getmode.cc
description:
### Description
When trying to install `fs` from source on a Windows ARM64 machine (Surface Laptop 7) using the new Rtools45 (clang compiler), the compilation fails due to a missing include for `EINVAL`. 

### Error Message
```text
aarch64-w64-mingw32.static.posix-clang++ -std=gnu++17 [...] -c windows/getmode.cc -o windows/getmode.o
windows/getmode.cc:50:13: error: use of undeclared identifier 'EINVAL'
   50 |     errno = EINVAL;
      |             ^
1 error generated.
ERROR: compilation failed for package 'fs'
```
### System Information
- OS: Windows 11 on ARM64 (Surface Laptop 7)
- R Version: 4.5.3 (arm64)
- Compiler: Rtools45 (aarch64-w64-mingw32.static.posix-clang++)

### Proposed Fix
Adding `#include <cerrno>` to the top of `src/windows/getmode.cc` resolves the issue and allows the package to compile successfully.

title: ext argument of fs::path is not vectorized
description:
I was surprised to find that the `ext` argument of `fs::path` is not vectorized, as demonstrated in the below example:

``` r
library(fs)
library(assertthat)

bad_paths <- path("foo", letters[1:3], ext = c("txt1", "txt2", "txt3"))
correct_paths <- paste0("foo/", letters[1:3], ".txt", 1:3)
assert_that(all(bad_paths == correct_paths))
#> Error: Elements 2, 3 of bad_paths == correct_paths are not true
```

<sup>Created on 2025-07-20 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

The function silently takes the first element of `ext` and uses it for all elements, which leads to unexpected behavior. Either the argument should be modified to accept a vector rather than a scalar, or if not being vectorized is intentional, then it should at least throw an error when passed a vector with length != 1, and this fact should be documented in the help text.

title: `dir_tree()` not listing files inside a directory inside `path` when glob or regexp is used
description:
Hi. I'm having a issue where I'm trying to list some zip files inside a directory in my project using `dir_tree()` and they're not showing up. I thought I was messing up with `glob` or `regexp`, but it doesn't seem to be the case, since `dir_ls()` works fine. Example below:

```r
library(fs)

dir_path <- tempfile("tmpdir")
dir.create(dir_path)

nested_dir <- file.path(dir_path, "nested_dir")
dir.create(nested_dir)

dir_tree(dir_path)
#> /tmp/RtmpCR1OTJ/tmpdir8bdf67c149e7
#> └── nested_dir

file.create(file.path(nested_dir, "a.zip"))
#> [1] TRUE
file.create(file.path(nested_dir, "b.zip"))
#> [1] TRUE

dir_tree(dir_path, recurse = TRUE, glob = "*.zip")
#> /tmp/RtmpCR1OTJ/tmpdir8bdf67c149e7

dir_ls(dir_path, recurse = TRUE, glob = "*.zip")
#> /tmp/RtmpCR1OTJ/tmpdir8bdf67c149e7/nested_dir/a.zip
#> /tmp/RtmpCR1OTJ/tmpdir8bdf67c149e7/nested_dir/b.zip

dir_tree(dir_path)
#> /tmp/RtmpCR1OTJ/tmpdir8bdf67c149e7
#> └── nested_dir
#>     ├── a.zip
#>     └── b.zip
```

You can see that both `a.zip` and `b.zip` are listed using `dir_ls()`, but this is not the case when using `dir_tree()`. I'd hope that the output of the first `dir_tree()` attempt would look like the second one, but that's not the case. I tried many different patterns (`"nested_dir/a.zip"`, `"*/*.zip"`, ...), but none seemed to work.

Not sure if this is intended behaviour or not, but I'd imagine that both `dir_tree()` and `dir_ls()` would output the same file list. Cheers!

title: `dir_copy()` gives diiferent results for `overwrite` parameter to empty destination
description:
When doing a `dir_copy()` to an empty destination folder the overwrite parameter produces different results. 

In the example below we create the `foo` dir that contains `sub1`. Then, we copy `foo` to newly created destinations `dest` and `dest_overwrite` with `overwrite = FALSE` and `overwrite = TRUE` respectively. I wouldn't expect the dir tree of the destination folders to defer, however, overwrite parameter affects the nesting of the directories

``` r
library(fs)

withr::with_tempdir({
  dir_create("foo")
  dir_create("foo/sub1")

  dir_create("dest")
  dir_copy("foo", "dest", overwrite = FALSE)

  dir_create("dest_overwrite")
  dir_copy("foo", "dest_overwrite", overwrite = TRUE)

  print(dir_tree("dest"))
  print(dir_tree("dest_overwrite"))
})
#> dest
#> └── foo
#>     └── sub1
#> dest/foo      dest/foo/sub1 
#> dest_overwrite
#> └── sub1
#> dest_overwrite/sub1
```

title: `file_chmod` doesn't work with an empty vector and a single mode
description:
It is quite common to call `file_chmod` with a vector of files and a single mode, which mostly works.
As a corner case however, the vector of files can be empty in which case an out-of-bounds is thrown. I would expect this to be allowed, and be a no-op.

```r
fs::file_chmod(character(0), "644")
#> Error in `[[.default`(mode, ((i + 1)%%length(mode)) + 1L) :
#>  subscript out of bounds

traceback()
#> 9: NextMethod("[[")
#> 8: unlist(list(...))
#> 7: assert("`x` must be an integer", is.integer(x))
#> 6: new_fs_perms(NextMethod("[["))
#> 5: `[[.fs_perms`(mode, ((i + 1)%%length(mode)) + 1L)
#> 4: mode[[((i + 1)%%length(mode)) + 1L]]
#> 3: as_fs_perms.character(mode, mode = file_info(path)$permissions)
#> 2: as_fs_perms(mode, mode = file_info(path)$permissions)
#> 1: fs::file_chmod(character(0), "644")
```

Similarly, if a single file path is given but the mode is empty, an out-of-bounds error is thrown. In this case I do expect an error, but it seems like it should get caught earlier with a nicer error message.
```r
fs::file_chmod(c("hello.txt"), character(0))
#> Error in res[[((i + 1)%%length(res)) + 1L]] : subscript out of bounds

traceback()
#> 3: as_fs_perms.character(mode, mode = file_info(path)$permissions)
#> 2: as_fs_perms(mode, mode = file_info(path)$permissions)
#> 1: fs::file_chmod(c("hello.txt"), character(0))
```

Conversely, the function accepts a single file path with a vector of modes, and uses the first element of the vector:
```r
fs::file_chmod("hello.txt", c("644", "755"))
fs::file_info("hello.txt")$permissions
#> [1] rw-r--r--
```

This behaviour seems nonsensical and in my opinion should throw an error.

title: `dir_copy` and permissions to the `new_path`
description:
Currently `dir_copy` uses `dir_create` internally to create destination folder. But it uses default permissions (default value of `mode` argument which is `"u=rwx,go=rx"`).

Shouldn't it copy the permissions from the original folder? Or at least give a way to change it (e.g. with `mode` argument passed on to `dir_create`)?

I came across this while copying results from one workflow to another and realized I was the only person on our team who could work with copied folders :/

title: dir_create() fails in ACL-controlled directories
description:
Following an upgrade from fs 1.5.0 to fs 1.6.4, downstream libraries such as batchtools and usethis began to return cryptic errors when attempting to create directories. We isolated the issue to the use of `fs::dir_create()` in ACL-controlled directories.

Specifically, we received the following result:
```>fs::dir_create('/working/temp')```
```Error: [EOI] Failed to make directory '/working/temp': i/o error```

The error occurred only in ACL-controlled directories, and it occurred only with fs 1.5.2 and higher.

I was able to resolve the error by modifying the default mode used in directory creation from `0x777` to `0x000` on [line 25 of dir.cc](https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/714990b50a9c8e2a9cae8bf6364c91636a712279/src/dir.cc#L25). After installing again from the modified source I was able to execute the above command without error.

We use R 4.4.1 on a linux server. Our server administrators tell us that the directories at issue use a GPFS file system with NFSv4 ACLs implemented by IBM. In addition, they report that directories *are* created after running the command above, with mode `1000`, but they are not accessible to users.

title: NFS caching causes `file_exists()` to return wrong result
description:
The `file_exists()` method relies on `stat()` to determine whether or not a file exists. Since `stat()` is subject to the NFS attribute cache, this information can easily be a full minute out of date. A more appropriate file existence test might be a call to `open()` followed by an immediate `close()`. This is not cached. Notably, the `open()`/`close()` sequence also _flushes_ the NFS cache, making a subsequent call to `access()` (`fs::file_access()`) or `stat()` (`fs::file_info()`) yield fresh results.

I would propose to change `file_exists()` to the open/close pattern, as here caching is both unexpected (other implementations use open/close to detect file presence) and not usually performance relevant. At least, I can't think of many scenarios where a API user would check for the existence of a million files. With `file_access()` and `file_info()` the situation is different, it is more obvious that this is meta data that may get cached (on NFS specifically) and these are more likely to be called on large input vectors or many times. The rest can be docs, and `file_exists` can also double as cache flush. Also, this is much less code change than an extra flag to all the functions and a dedicated cache flush function.

(Happy to do PR to this effect if desired)

title: When `ext` is a vector, `path()` recycles only the first value
description:
`path()` of `... ` can be given a vector, but when `ext` is given a vector, only the first value is recycled.
I think some fix is needed, since users are likely to expect the result of `purrr::map2_vec()` shown in reprex.

``` r

title: suggestion: overload `/` for pathlib-like path construction
description:
I've been using python a lot lately and have come to love the intuitiveness of the division operator in `pathlib`:

```python
import pathlib

parent = pathlib.Path('parent')

parent / 'child'
## PosixPath('parent/child')
```

I think `fs` is the closest analog to `pathlib`, and similar overloading could be implemented like this:

```r
library(fs)

parent <- path("somedir")

# base errors
parent / "somefile"
#> Error in parent/"somefile": non-numeric argument to binary operator
parent + "somefile"
#> Error in parent + "somefile": non-numeric argument to binary operator

Ops.fs_path <- function(parent, child) {
  if (.Generic == "/") {
    path_join(c(parent, child))
  } else {
    NextMethod(.Generic, parent)
  }
}

# works!
parent / "somefile"
#> somedir/somefile
class(parent / "somefile")
#> [1] "fs_path"   "character"

# also works
parent / 1
#> somedir/1

# not quite same as before
parent + "somefile"
#> Error in `+.default`(parent, "somefile"): non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

(I suspect `NextMethod` should be something else to more exactly preserve the base error message, but I'm not sure what; my OO-foo is weak. I just know _something_ needs to be there to prevent `NULL`s being returned for each unhandled generic.)

Is this worthy of inclusion in `fs`? If so I'd gladly submit a PR with tests and such.

title: New folders are created with `0755` permission
description:
I'm aware of the discussion here https://github.com/r-lib/fs/issues/293

Today I encountered this issue. I was running an R script on my server. I set my system default umask to be `077` (https://support.apple.com/en-us/101914), and `Sys.umask()` is "77", hoping that the code would respect that (I also have ACL set up on the project folder so normally only the code owner and user group permitted by ACL can run commands. However, packages depending on `fs` generated bunch of `0755` files (because my account has the admin (not root) privilege).

This incident raised my concerns. You see the people who wrote the code might not be the same group of people who actually run the code, especially for R package authors. Most people who use `fs` because it is a powerful substitute (indeed it is) to the base functions. It has almost no learning curve. People who are already familiar with base functions can easily transfer to `fs` **with no significant differences**

However, such "naive" assumption might cause problems. The code authors might not know how chmod, umask, ACL work (they don't need to). People who know the permissions might also give upthinking and rely on `fs` being consistent (since `fs` is too similar to base functions and too easy to use). 

My suggestion is maybe `fs` always respect `Sys.umask`, and can be turned off via `options`. For most users this won't change their experience as most system default umask is 022.

Alternatively users can instruct whether to respect `Sys.umask` by wrapping the mode

```
fs::dir_create("dir", mode = "0777", umask = Sys.umask())

# or

fs::dir_create("dir", mode = fs::safe_mode("0777"))
safe_mode <- function(mode, umask = Sys.umask()) {
  ...
}
```

Then all the code that tries to change to mode to `0777` is constrained by user-controlled umask

title: Optionally let `dir_tree` hide parent directories (like `lsd --tree`)
description:
I am writing a quarto book on data management, and I need to show a certain directory structure. The easiest way of course is to create this structure and then to use `fs::dir_tree()` to get it to show in the book, however this will show all my parent directories up until the quarto book root directory (because the working directory cannot be changed on a per-chunk basis, I tried that first).

Coincidentally this is also the difference between `/bin/tree` and `lsd --tree` (https://github.com/lsd-rs/lsd), so more people might prefer this format, see the example code below:

``` r
library(fs)

fs::dir_create("a/b/c/d/e")

# adapted from fs::dir_tree
# Option to hide the parent directories e.g.,
# my_dir_tree("a/b/c") will show "c" as top node, whereas fs::dir_tree will show "a/b/c" as top node
my_dir_tree <- function (path = ".", recurse = TRUE, ...)
{
  files <- fs::dir_ls(path, recurse = recurse, ...)
  by_dir <- split(files, fs::path_dir(files))
  ch <- fs:::box_chars()
  get_coloured_name <- function(x) {
    coloured <- fs:::colourise_fs_path(x)
    sub(x, fs::path_file(x), coloured, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  print_leaf <- function(x, indent) {
    leafs <- by_dir[[x]]
    for (i in seq_along(leafs)) {
      if (i == length(leafs)) {
        cat(indent, fs:::pc(ch$l, ch$h, ch$h, " "), get_coloured_name(leafs[[i]]),
            "\n", sep = "")
        print_leaf(leafs[[i]], paste0(indent, "    "))
      }
      else {
        cat(indent, fs:::pc(ch$j, ch$h, ch$h, " "), get_coloured_name(leafs[[i]]),
            "\n", sep = "")
        print_leaf(leafs[[i]], paste0(indent, pc(ch$v, "   ")))
      }
    }
  }
  cat(sub(path, fs::path_file(path), fs:::colourise_fs_path(path), fixed = T), "\n", sep = "")
  print_leaf(fs::path_expand(path), "")
  invisible(files)
}

my_dir_tree("a/b/c")
#> c
#> └── d
#>     └── e
fs::dir_tree("a/b/c")
#> a/b/c
#> └── d
#>     └── e

fs::dir_delete("a")
```

<sup>Created on 2024-02-09 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

If this is something that could be added with an option to the `dir_tree()` command, I'd be happy to create a pull request

title: Providing `pattern` to dir_ls() silently gives wrong result
description:
``` r
library(fs)

dir_ls()
#> DESCRIPTION                        LICENSE                            
#> LICENSE.md                         NAMESPACE                          
#> NEWS.md                            R                                  
#> README.Rmd                         README.md                          
#> _pkgdown.yml                       codecov.yml                        
#> cran-comments.md                   fs.Rproj                           
#> inst                               man                                
#> man-roxygen                        reprex72c8745a53e2_reprex.R        
#> reprex72c8745a53e2_reprex.spin.R   reprex72c8745a53e2_reprex.spin.Rmd 
#> revdep                             src                                
#> tests                              vignettes

dir_ls(regexp = "[.]yml$")
#> _pkgdown.yml codecov.yml

dir_ls(pattern = "[.]yml$")
#> DESCRIPTION                        LICENSE                            
#> LICENSE.md                         NAMESPACE                          
#> NEWS.md                            R                                  
#> README.Rmd                         README.md                          
#> _pkgdown.yml                       codecov.yml                        
#> cran-comments.md                   fs.Rproj                           
#> inst                               man                                
#> man-roxygen                        reprex72c8745a53e2_reprex.R        
#> reprex72c8745a53e2_reprex.spin.R   reprex72c8745a53e2_reprex.spin.Rmd 
#> revdep                             src                                
#> tests                              vignettes
```

<sup>Created on 2021-01-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0.9000)</sup>

It's very easy for people to provide their filtering regex to `dir_ls()` via `pattern` à la `list.files()`, when what they really mean is `regexp`. And then `pattern` gets silently swallowed by `...` in `dir_ls()` and `path_filter()`, resulting in no filtering at all. The docs say that `...` gets passed along to `grep()`, but that doesn't happen in this case.

Discovered while debugging a puzzling error in usethis (https://github.com/r-lib/usethis/issues/1336).

title: fs::file_info hangs for symlinks of symlinks
description:
It seems like `fs::is_file('/opt/homebrew/bin/python3')` hangs on Mac with homebrew python installed. This doesn't seem to be a Mac specific bug because I was able to reproduce it by recreating the folder structure and symlinks on a linux computer I have.

# Steps to reproduce

Create symlinks and folder structure with the script below
```sh
mkdir -p opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.11/3.11.6_1/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.11/bin
cd opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.11/3.11.6_1/Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.11/bin
echo "#!/bin/sh
echo 'hi'
" > python3.11
chmod +x python3.11
ln -s python3.11 python3
cd ../../../../../../../../../../
mkdir -p opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.11/3.11.6_1/bin
cd opt/homebrew/Cellar/python@3.11/3.11.6_1/bin
ln -s ../Frameworks/Python.framework/Versions/3.11/bin/python3 python3
cd ../../../../../../
mkdir -p opt/homebrew/bin
cd opt/homebrew/bin
ln -s ../Cellar/python@3.11/3.11.6_1/bin/python3 python3
cd ../../../
```

And then run `fs::is_file('opt/homebrew/bin/python3')` to see it hangs.

# Version Information

```
$ R --version
R version 4.1.2 (2021-11-01) -- "Bird Hippie"
Copyright (C) 2021 The R Foundation for Statistical Computing
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)
```

I installed the version of fs from GitHub, which is at 8a84fc9 at the time of writing.

title: Support for `path("http://", ...)`
description:

## Expected Behavior

I expected a return value of 'https://github.com/r-lib/fs/issues', similar to the output of `file.path("https://github.com/r-lib/fs", "issues")` from base R.

title: `file_move()` and `file_delete()` did not work recursively
description:
It is very common to use `dir_ls()` with `glob` or `regexp` to filter some files and move them into a target directory. However, `file_move()` did not work recursively. Neither did `file_delete()`. The reason for the error `file_delete()` is straightforward, since it runs `dir_delete()` on all directories first, then all file unlink.

Is this the expected behavior? If so, what is the suggested way to handle file moving or deleting recursively using {fs}? Thanks!

``` r
get_files <- function() {
    fs::dir_create("dir1/dir2")
    fs::file_create(fs::path("dir1/dir2", letters[1:5]))
    fs::dir_ls("dir1", recurse = TRUE)
}

fs::dir_create("dir3")
fs::file_move(get_files(), "dir3")
#> Error: [ENOENT] Failed to move 'dir1/dir2/a'to 'dir3/a': no such file or directory

fs::file_delete(get_files())
#> Error: [ENOENT] Failed to remove 'dir1/dir2/a': no such file or directory

file.remove(get_files()) # base::file.remove only works for files
#> Warning in file.remove(get_files()): cannot remove file 'dir1/dir2', reason
#> 'Permission denied'
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
unlink(get_files()) # base::unlink() works
```

title: Can `<fs_bytes>` force you towards using `<double>` as the internal storage type?
description:
See https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/issues/1806

I think we'd need to move away from using the "union" type of `<numeric>` in favor of explicitly handling integer and double separately.

Like here, where we'd `as.double()` an integer vector:
https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/2fe50ea934967804f0644b5e0cc55c962419c529/R/fs_bytes.R#L54-L56

And around here where we'd `vec_cast(to = integer())` after unclassing
https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/2fe50ea934967804f0644b5e0cc55c962419c529/R/fs_bytes.R#L183-L188

And the class we put on it should probably be `"double"` (this is also done in the C code)

https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/2fe50ea934967804f0644b5e0cc55c962419c529/R/fs_bytes.R#L31-L35

title: Is dropping of attributes by fs::path intentional?
description:
`fs` operations like `fs::path` or `fs::path_rel` remove attributes from paths, in particular names.
Is this intended / Are attributes other than `"class"` considered untidy?
This seems to be in contrast to the advice given in [R-internals](
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-ints.html#Attributes). 

Full example:
``` r
my_paths <- c("A" = "/home/jan/a", "B" = "/home/jan/b")
attributes(my_paths)$note <- "remember me"

my_paths_rel <- fs::path_rel(my_paths, start = "/home/jan")

str(my_paths_rel) # current behaviour
#>  'fs_path' chr [1:2] "a" "b"


collapse::copyAttrib(my_paths_rel, from = my_paths)
#>   A   B 
#> "a" "b" 
#> attr(,"note")
#> [1] "remember me"
class(my_paths_rel) <- c("fs_path", class(my_paths_rel))
str(my_paths_rel) # behaviour expected by me
#>  'fs_path' Named chr [1:2] "a" "b"
#>  - attr(*, "names")= chr [1:2] "A" "B"
#>  - attr(*, "note")= chr "remember me"
```

title: `dir_copy()` is not idempotent when `overwrite = F`
description:
The results of a second execution of `dir_copy()` when `overwrite = F` are not as I expected. I expected an error message, but instead it copied the source directory into the target, but nested one level deeper than during the first execution. 

Here's an example

```r
library(fs)

# create test source directory
dir_create("a/b")
file_create("a/b/test.txt")
dir_tree("a")

# a
# └── b
#     └── test.txt

# first copy: contents of 'a' are copied to 'c' = c/b/test.txt
# this is what I expected
dir_copy("a", "c", overwrite = F)
dir_tree("c")

# c
# └── b
#     └── test.txt

# second copy: 'a' and it's contents are copied to 'c' = c/a/b/test.txt
# expected: error about overwriting
# this is the step that seems incorrect to me
dir_copy("a", "c", overwrite = F)
dir_tree("c")

# c
# ├── a
# │   └── b
# │       └── test.txt
# └── b
#     └── test.txt

# third copy: error about overwriting
dir_copy("a", "c", overwrite = F)
# Error: [EEXIST] Failed to copy 'a/b/test.txt' to 'c/a/b/test.txt': file already exists

# test with overwrite = T

# first copy - same results as before: d/b/test.txt
dir_copy("a", "d", overwrite = T)
dir_tree("d")

# d
# └── b
#     └── test.txt

# second copy - expected results: silent overwrite
dir_copy("a", "d", overwrite = T)
dir_tree("d")

# d
# └── b
#     └── test.txt

# cleanup
dir_delete("a")
dir_delete("c")
dir_delete("d")
```

title: fs::path_dir is significantly slower on Windows vs Mac
description:
When you use `read_csv(..., id="file_path")` you end up with a `file_path` column that has lots of repeats. Manipulations on this kind of column are somewhat slow. I have found that it's much faster to do a `left_join(x, distinct(x, file_path) |> mutate(...), by="file_path")` than it is to do the mutate directly.

Below I timed using `fs::path_dir` directly (with no tibble involvement at all) compared to going via a tibble to do the above. Even though the latter is significantly more indirect, it's more than 13X faster:

``` r
paths <- fs::path("base", stringr::str_glue("dir{d}", d=1:10), "inner") |> 
  rep(1e3)

bench::mark(
  direct = fs::path_dir(paths),
  indirect = {
    x <- tibble::tibble(a = paths)
    dplyr::left_join(x, dplyr::distinct(x, a) |> dplyr::mutate(b = fs::path_dir(a)), 
                     by = "a") |> 
      dplyr::pull(b)
  },
  iterations = 50
)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 direct      54.05ms  55.66ms      17.9  749.02KB    0.746
#> 2 indirect     3.68ms   4.14ms     237.     6.47MB    9.86
```

title: split off the plotting piece of dir_tree()?
description:
I'm looking for a nice way to display graph and/or tree structures in the terminal for when regular plots are not available, and `dir_tree()` is the first thing I came across that seems to do the job reasonably well (googling has proven a bit hard, though, as most searches seem to think I want the `text()` method for some other object).

Would it make sense to split off the plotting part of `dir_tree()` into a separate function to abstract away its dependence on files? Or maybe to put that part into a separate package?

I could hack together a way to fake the directory structure in `tempdir()` but that seems quite goldbergian.

title: Feature Request: `link_create()` on Windows networked drives
description:
Hello! Thank you for this wonderful package. :postbox:

Is it possible for `link_create()` to be updated to create symlinks to mapped network drives on Windows? I think the reason it's not already available is that it may require admin access as mentioned by Jim Hester in another issue for `link_create()` (comment copied below)? This issue is from 2018...perhaps libuv has now been updated to optionally not require admin access? 

Thank you! :relaxed:

https://github.com/r-lib/fs/issues/79
> `fs::link_create()` currently uses junctions on windows, which only support linking directories. This is because the Windows API requires the process to be elevated as administrator to create symbolic links (for both files and directories) using the [`CreateSymbolicLink()`](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/windows/desktop/aa363866(v=vs.85).aspx) API. Recent versions of Windows 10 insiders builds include an option `SYMBOLIC_LINK_FLAG_ALLOW_UNPRIVILEGED_CREATE` to create symlinks without privelage elevation which is supported in libuv as of [libuv/libuv@89d3193](https://github.com/libuv/libuv/commit/89d31932a595fdec18dd19b70142816312ea2338), however currently we are using an older version of libuv in this package.

title: `dir_ls()` trips over non-ascii file names when native encoding isn't UTF-8
description:
Discovered while studying https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/1345.

`dir_map()` (on the C/C++ side) seems to assume libuv is giving it UTF-8 paths, but that's not true on Windows (where I made this reprex).

``` r
library(fs)
library(testthat)

twd <- path_temp(pattern = "dir-ls-reprex")
dir_create(twd)
owd <- setwd(twd)

cat("blah\n", file = "äçé")

(native <- list.files())
#> [1] "äçé"
(from_fs <- dir_ls())
#> Ã¤Ã§Ã©

# this mojibake is erroneously marked as UTF-8
Encoding(from_fs)
#> [1] "UTF-8"

# here are the bytes I'm expecting
(correct <- iconv(native, to = "UTF-8"))
#> [1] "äçé"

local({
  local_edition(3)
  expect_equal(
    charToRaw(correct),
    charToRaw(from_fs)
  )
})
#> Error: charToRaw(correct) (`actual`) not equal to charToRaw(from_fs) (`expected`).
#> 
#> `actual`:   "c3" "a4" "c3" "a7" "c3" "a9"                     and 2 more...
#> `expected`: "c3" "83" "c2" "a4" "c3" "83" "c2" "a7" "c3" "83" ...

setwd(owd)
dir_delete(twd)
#> Error: [ENOENT] Failed to remove 'C:/Users/jenny/AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpeEIdP0/dir-ls-reprex/ÃƒÂ¤ÃƒÂ§ÃƒÂ©': no such file or directory
```

<sup>Created on 2022-01-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

For some meta points, I think the `dir_ls()` bug is also why I can't use fs to delete the temp directory in this reprex.

title: path_expand has trouble with special characters in the expanded bit under Windows (not UTF8)
description:
`path_expand()` handles special characters, except when they are in the expanded part. Here is a MRE in a non-UTF8 Windows 10 system.

``` r
## I have a funny user name
Sys.getenv("HOME")
#> [1] "C:\\Users\\Facundo Muñoz\\Documents"

## path_expand() understands special characters
fs::path_expand( "C:/Users/Facundo Muñoz/")
#> C:/Users/Facundo Muñoz

## but they cause trouble when expanded
fs::path_expand("~/")  # as in fs::path_home()
#> Error in base::nchar(x, type, allowNA, keepNA) : 
#>   invalid multibyte string, element 1

## this is how the function works
fs::path_expand
#> function (path) 
#> {
#>     path <- enc2utf8(path)
#>     path_tidy(.Call(fs_expand_, path, Sys.getenv("R_FS_HOME") != 
#>         "" || is_windows()))
#> }
#> <bytecode: 0x5621b217fdb0>
#> <environment: namespace:fs>

## in the first case, the string is encoded previously
## and the special character is preserved
.Call(fs:::fs_expand_, enc2utf8("Muñoz"), TRUE)
#> [1] "Muñoz"

## in the second case, the path is expanded afterwards
## and the special character is scrambled
.Call(fs:::fs_expand_, "~", TRUE)
#> "C:/Users/Facundo Mu\xf1oz"
```

title: Copy directory tree but only keeping some files (e.g. CSVs)
description:
I have a server with data saved in a particular folder structure with CSV files I care about and others I don't, like images that take up a lot of space. I want to copy only the CSV files locally to my computer, but keep the directory structure so that I can then run the same analysis directly on the server.

I don't think there's a way of doing this easily with any current `fs` function, other than to write my own looping function that uses `dir_create` and `file_copy`. It would be great if there was either a new function that does this. I'd think it should either interface with the results of `dir_ls` (e.g. `dir_ls(...) %>% dir_select_copy()`) or have the same method signature as `dir_ls`.

title: path_tidy breaks paths with backslashes in them
description:
I'm on Linux, and I'm dealing with some paths that, for reasons unknown to me, contain backslashes in the file names. It seems that the fs package abjectly refuses to admit the existence of backslashes:

``` r
library(fs)
library(assertthat)
myfile <- tempfile("path with a back\\slash")
system(paste("touch", shQuote(myfile)))
assert_that(file.exists(myfile))
#> [1] TRUE
## Fails
assert_that(file_exists(myfile))
#> Error: file_exists(path = myfile) is not TRUE

myfile_tidy <- path_tidy(myfile)
print(myfile_tidy)
#> /var/folders/dt/6dg7l6491fjdpb17tfgld9rc0000gn/T/RtmpHj4ctg/path with a back/slash62c12c0f5718
regex_matching_one_backslash <- "\\\\"
assert_that(grepl(regex_matching_one_backslash, myfile))
#> [1] TRUE
## Fails
assert_that(grepl(regex_matching_one_backslash, myfile_tidy))
#> Error: grepl(pattern = regex_matching_one_backslash, x = myfile_tidy) is not TRUE
```
<sup>Created on 2022-07-21 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I'm guessing the package is trying to enforce the same path separator for UNIX and Windows systems, but does this mean that paths with backslashes in them are simply not supported at all?

title: Invalid multibyte string when printing certain combination of characters with fs::path()
description:
This is an issue that emerges when a certain, admittedly unusual, combination of valid characters is printed on the console via `fs::path()`. The shortest combination I found is the following (with the relevant error): 

```
fs::path("śl")
```
> Error in base::nchar(x, type, allowNA, keepNA) : 
  invalid multibyte string, element 1

The issue does not seem to be related to the `ś` itself, as the following works nicely:

```
fs::path("ś")
```
Obvious solutions such as the following all return the same error:

```
fs::path(stringi::stri_enc_toutf8("śl"))
fs::path(stringi::stri_enc_tonative("śl"))
fs::path(fs::path_sanitize("śl"))
```
> Error in base::nchar(x, type, allowNA, keepNA) : 
  invalid multibyte string, element 1

If you look at the reprex, all seemingly works fine. But if I run the same code on the console, then I get the above error. 

I include a reprex for reference, as well as a screenshot, since the issue is not fully visible via reprex.

In the real world,  this issue emerges as I print `fs::path()` as a form to show advancement in a script that processes data related to a bunch of cities, including the Polish city of [Przemyśl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Przemy%C5%9Bl).

Of course there are ways around it, but since it broke my scripts, I still decided to report this.  Tested with both the current development version (see reprex below) and version currently on CRAN (1.5.2)



``` r
library("fs")

# see e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Przemy%C5%9Bl
x <- "Przemyśl"

# works
print(x)
#> [1] "Przemyśl"

# throws error
fs::path(x)
#> Przemyśl

# throws error
fs::path(stringi::stri_enc_toutf8(x))
#> Przemyśl

# works
fs::path_sanitize(filename = x) 
#> [1] "Przemyśl"

# throws error
fs::path(fs::path_sanitize(filename = x))
#> Przemyśl

# works
y <- invisible(fs::path(x))

# works
stringr::str_c(y)
#> [1] "Przemyśl"

# works
filename <- fs::path(tempdir(), "Przemyśl.txt")

# throws error
fs::path(filename)
#> /tmp/RtmpzO4Dt3/Przemyśl.txt

# works
writeLines("test", fs::path(filename))

# works
fs::path("ś")
#> ś

# works
fs::path("Przemyś")
#> Przemyś

# throws error
fs::path("śl")

title: dir_ls() glob does not work with subfolders
description:
Hi,

I am on Windows using `dir_ls()` to walk through all my csv files across various subfolders in a main folder.

For example, the base directory for the following example is `C:\\Users\\mainfolder\\`, and I use the `*` to represent all subfolders. There is a `report` folder in every subfolder storing all csv files. (Note: the path I set here is the absolute one.)
`dir_ls("C:\\Users\\mainfolder\\", glob = "*\\report\\*.csv", recurse = T) `

It seems like `glob` does not take two `*`s. Any solutions for this issue? Thanks!

title: Handling of URL encoded paths
description:
Should URL encoded paths be handled by fs functions or is that not possible/desirable? Apologies if a stupid question!

For example, when there are spaces in folder names:
```{r}
folder_path <- "~/foo bar/image.png"
encoded_folder_path <- utils::URLencode(folder_path)

fs::path_rel(folder_path, encoded_folder_path)
# doesn't give the same result as
fs::path_rel(folder_path, folder_path)
```

I only ask because I'm having an issue with a pkgdown site, when building vignettes (i.e. `pkgdown::build_article()`): 
- `rmarkdown::render()` encodes image src paths as URLs, because an output_dir is set
- `pkgdown:::tweak_rmarkdown_html()` uses `fs::path_rel()` to replace absolute paths with relative paths
-  So image src paths are being converted to something like '../../../../../../../../../../{full url encoded path}'
-  I'm getting an error saying my file paths are too long

I can see three possibilities
1) `fs::path_rel` can/should handle URL encoded paths
2) there is/should be an option for rmarkdown to avoid URL encoding image src paths?
3) neither of the above is possible/desirable for some reason and it is just an unavoidable side effect of me having long file paths with spaces in

I'm not sure which of these is true (if any) so any help is much appreciated! Also if this isn't the right place for this question let me know, happy to post somewhere else instead if necessary.

title: fs::file_exists returns false for existing files on Window
description:
Hi.  The boxr package caches an oauth token in the file \~/.boxr-oauth.  During a forced refresh, the code uses fs::file_exists to check if the token exists.  However, on windows, even though the \~/.boxr-oauth file exist, file_exists return false.  

I don't believe this is caused by the '.', because when in the ~ directory on windows file_exists works correctly.  This is not a path expansion problem, because `fs::file_exists(fs::path_expand("~/.boxr-oauth"))` returns false. 

The issue in the boxr repository is https://github.com/r-box/boxr/issues/219.  It contains the session info. 

Happy to provide more details if needed.

title: Inconsistent treatment of non-character path inputs
description:
Some functions (e.g. `path_tidy`) call `enc2utf8(as.character(path))`, but others do not coerce to character first (e.g. `path_expand` just calls `enc2utf8(path)`). This leads to inconsistent treatment of non-character path inputs between different functions:
```
> fs::path_tidy(NA)
NA
> fs::path_expand(NA)
Error in enc2utf8(path) : argument is not a character vector
```

and also logically-inconsistent behaviour in some cases:
```
> fs::file_exists(NA_character_)
 <NA> 
FALSE 
```
but
```
> fs::file_exists(NA)
Error in enc2utf8(path) : argument is not a character vector
```

If this isn't intentional, would it be unreasonable to apply an `as.character` coercion to all calls to `enc2utf8` to avoid these errors?

#> ~/any_file 
#> FALSE 
base::file.exists(any_file_path)
#> TRUE
```

path_dir constructs the whole path using sysenv "HOME" while file_exists seems to look into "HOMEPATH"

I know that i can work arround this by using `path_expand()` and `path_expand_r()`
but that behavior isn't very intuitive. Because `fs::file_create()` also creates within sysenv "HOMEPATH".

Maybe you could add some options which path should be referred to when `~` is involved.

Cheers, and great package so far! I absolutely love it :)

title: fs operations for file path URIs
description: The [File URI scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File_URI_scheme) is recognized by base R functions, but not `fs` functions. title: `file_create()` and `dir_create()` return wrong path
description:
According to the [documentation](https://fs.r-lib.org/reference/create.html), `file_create()` and `dir_create()` are supposed to return

> The path to the created object (invisibly).

However, instead they return the `path` argument. When `...` arguments have been used, this is not the same as the path to the created object. I think this might have been introduced by https://github.com/r-lib/fs/commit/6ee3322076bd2cb6b9cacd0b52ac1717b11996e4.

``` r
library(fs)

out_path <- file_create(tempdir(), "foo.txt")
out_path
#> /var/folders/pn/sn7ybdms78x_1pgjr17pv8v40000gn/T/RtmpfZdUtx

out_path <- dir_create(tempdir(), "foo", "bar")
out_path
#> /var/folders/pn/sn7ybdms78x_1pgjr17pv8v40000gn/T/RtmpfZdUtx
```

title: Should dir_walk have a glob argument?
description:
It's not obvious to me why `dir_walk` and `dir_map` lack the `glob` and `pattern` argument present in the other list functions (`dir_ls()` and friends).  

For example, I'd like to have travis check if all Rmds can render in a given git repo.  

Something like: 

```r
fs::dir_walk(glob = "*.Rmd", fun = rmarkdown::render,  recursive = TRUE)
```

seems like a nice alternative to:


```r
lapply(list.files(pattern = ".*.Rmd", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE), rmarkdown::render)
```

In general, I can imagine many other scenarios where I'd want to walk a directory for it's side effect based on a globbing pattern.  Maybe I'm just failing to understand the logic of `dir_walk` and `dir_map`, but they seem like attractive alternatives to piping `dir_ls()` version into a `purrr` function (and thus introducing a `purrr` dependency).

title: Relationship between umask and created directory permissions
description:
Hello. 

I am trying to understand the relationship between umask and the permissions created directories have.

I expected `dir_create` to follow the system umask setting (like shell `mkdir path` or `base::dir.create`) but it seems to follow the specified default `mode`. I think it would be great for `dir_create` to follow the umask setting so that I don't need to modify each call but maybe there is a good reason I don't understand for why `fs` was set up this way.

Thank you!

```
library(fs)
library(glue)
library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)

test_dir <- tempdir()

# Create directories three ways -------------------------------------------

Sys.umask(2)
fs::dir_create(fs::path(test_dir, "test_fs"))

Sys.umask(2)
base::dir.create(fs::path(test_dir, "test_base"))

Sys.umask(2)
mkdir_path <- fs::path(test_dir, "test_mkdir")
system(
  command = glue::glue("
  umask 002
  mkdir {mkdir_path}
  ")
)

# Get info on permissions of test directories -----------------------------

fs::dir_info(test_dir) %>%
  mutate(directory = fs::path_file(path)) %>%
  filter(grepl("test", directory)) %>%
  select(directory, permissions)

title: Feature request: dir_tree() with argument icon = TRUE
description:
Hi - I was wondering if `fs::dir_tree()` could gain an argument `icon = c(FALSE, TRUE)` where the display of an 
item is added, e.g.: 

```
#reprex setup
library(tidyverse)

fs::dir_create("test_dir")
fs::file_create("test_dir/test_file.R")

#capture output
test_tree <- capture.output(fs::dir_tree("test_dir"))

#desired output
test_tree %>% 
  str_replace_all(., "── test_file.R", "── 📝test_file.R") %>%
  str_replace_all(., "test_dir", "📁test_dir") %>% 
  tibble::enframe()

#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>    name value            
#>   <int> <chr>            
#> 1     1 📁test_dir       
#> 2     2 └── 📝test_file.R
```
For regular READMEs the coloured output of `fs::dir_tree()` is perfect but for presentations with non-tech-people I usually end up adding the icons manually - thats where this idea comes from.

If this breaks the idea of `fs`, no worries - thanks for your great work! `fs` is one of my top-5-workflow-packages!

title: Feature request: New function `path_glue()`
description:
I often find myself using `path()` along with `stringr::str_glue()` (or `glue::glue()`) to create paths from variables whilst ensuring they are clean and easy to work with.

This ends up with messy looking nested code, I wonder if the functionality of glue (specifically the ability to embed variables with `{}`) could be included in fs? Alternatively, it could be an additional argument to `path()`, `glue = FALSE` by default, which would have the behaviour described when set to TRUE.

title: Add `sort` argument
description:
I believe adding a `sort` argument to `dir_tree()` would be a nice, although not critical, addition to {fs}. (maybe skip `dir_tree()` and add directly to `dir_ls()`/`dir_map()`?)

### Example

A project like

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/67562667/120928983-a47eb380-c6d6-11eb-9038-709cc62a8486.png)

with a `dir_tree("my-project")` representation

```r
## my-project
## ├── R
## │   └── functions.R
## ├── analysis.R
## ├── my-project.Rproj
## ├── data
## ├── extra
## └── output
```

can be sorted in RStudio by "type" (the default is by "name")

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/67562667/120929065-063f1d80-c6d7-11eb-8fa3-76ad300600dd.png)

It would be great if `dir_tree("my-project", sort = "type")` worked like

```r
## my-project
## ├── data
## ├── extra
## ├── output
## ├── R
## │   └── functions.R
## ├── my-project.Rproj
## └── analysis.R
```

title: Move `master` branch to `main`
description:
The `master` branch of this repository will soon be renamed to `main`, as part of a coordinated change across several GitHub organizations (including, but not limited to: [tidyverse](https://github.com/tidyverse), [r-lib](https://github.com/r-lib), [tidymodels](https://github.com/tidymodels), and [sol-eng](https://github.com/sol-eng)). We anticipate this will happen by the end of September 2021.

That will be preceded by a release of the [usethis package](https://usethis.r-lib.org), which will gain some functionality around detecting and adapting to a renamed default branch. There will also be a blog post at the time of this `master` --> `main` change.

The purpose of this issue is to:

* Help us firm up the list of targetted repositories
* Make sure all maintainers are aware of what's coming
* Give us an issue to close when the job is done
* Give us a place to put advice for collaborators re: how to adapt

*message id: euphoric_snowdog*

title: Question: `fs::file_copy` vs `file.copy` speed on Windows network drive
description:
I noticed that using base `file.copy` on Windows to copy to a network file share is very slow (50 times slower) compared to `fs::file_copy`. Does anybody know why this would be the case? Does it suggest a method of improving base R performance for this core operation?

In the example I was looking at, a 200 MB file took about 50 minutes to transfer with `file.copy` and about 1 minute with `fs::file_copy`. In the file share metrics, it appeared `file.copy` performed many small transactions, but `fs::file_copy` performed a few larger transactions. This was using a mounted cloud-based SMB Azure file share on Windows.

I found this question on StackOverflow where a comment suggest it may relate to `file.copy` using a small buffer size: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49888078/copying-files-over-network-much-slower-with-file-copy-than-systemmv

Thanks in advance! I appreciate any help!

**Edit:**
It looks like maybe libuv is using a buffer of 65536 (http://docs.libuv.org/en/v1.x/handle.html)? I found it is possible to significantly speed up `file.copy` by increasing `BUFSIZ` from 512 to 65536 . Copying a 100MB file locally, the `file.copy` execution time is reduced from 398 ms to 72 ms. That is at least in the same ballpark as `fs::file_copy` at 62 ms. 

I would appreciate any insights, but realize I am probably a bit off topic now and should maybe open an issue for R.

```
Index: src/main/platform.c
===================================================================
--- src/main/platform.c	(revision 81244)
+++ src/main/platform.c	(working copy)
@@ -515,13 +515,13 @@
  *  the second set of files to be appended to the first.
  */
 
-#if defined(BUFSIZ) && (BUFSIZ > 512)
+#if defined(BUFSIZ) && (BUFSIZ > 65536)
 /* OS's buffer size in stdio.h, probably.
    Windows has 512, Solaris 1024, glibc 8192
  */
 # define APPENDBUFSIZE BUFSIZ
 #else
-# define APPENDBUFSIZE 512
+# define APPENDBUFSIZE 65536
 #endif
 
 static int R_AppendFile(SEXP file1, SEXP file2)
```

title: Unclear documentation of `link_create()`
description:
In `link_create(path, new_path, symbolic = TRUE)`, it's not clear to me which is the `path` and which is the `new_path`. In `bash`'s `ln`, it's documented as `ln -s TARGET LINK_NAME` which I find much more clear. In particular, it's not clear which path is the _new_ path: the location of the newly created link or the location that it points to.

If you think that a change should be made, I'm happy to do a PR.

Thanks for `fs` I use it all the time.

title: An improper locking due to the unreleased lock global_epoll_lock
description:
Hi developers, in the below codes, the lock `global_epoll_lock` could be not released before program's exit `abort(); `. I think there is no harm to write `uv_mutex_unlock(&global_epoll_lock);`  before the `abort(); ` for better resource management and code symmetry. Thanks!

https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/0895f1a897ebf3e1c7a2223438fad6313a1e3f1f/src/libuv-1.38.1/src/unix/os390-syscalls.c#L241-L276

title: Coercing `fs_bytes` to `character` when vector length > 1 pads character with space.
description:
When coercing `fs_bytes` vector to a `character` vector, some of the characters are padded with a space. This seems to only happen when the vector has a length greater than 1. I was unable to find in the documentation that this is expected behavior, nor was I able to find a similar issue open, but please feel free to correct me.

```r
library(fs)

# Simple Example ----
# 24.1K has a space in front of it
as.character(fs::fs_bytes(c("24.1K", "437")))
[1] " 24.1K" "437"

# Another Example ----

# Get paths to two files
path_copyright <- fs::path_package("fs", "COPYRIGHTS")
path_wordlist <- fs::path_package("fs", "WORDLIST")

# Get file info on each path
info_copyright <- fs::file_info(path_copyright)
info_wordlist <- fs::file_info(path_wordlist)
info_both <- fs::file_info(c(path_copyright, path_wordlist))

# Show size of each, individualy
info_copyright$size # 24.1K
info_wordlist$size  # 437
info_both$size      # 24.1K 437

# Cast as.character
char_copyright <- as.character(info_copyright$size) # 24.1K
char_wordlist <- as.character(info_wordlist$size)   # 437

# Check equality
c(char_copyright, char_wordlist) == char_both

# Check fix equality
c(char_copyright, char_wordlist) == gsub(" ", "", char_both)

title: shortening `fs_path` content when printing tibbles
description:
Hi and thanks for the great package! If this feature is already available in some manner, my apologies.

I'd like to (optionally) shorten the display of `fs_path` objects in a vector when they're long, so that the ellipsis is on the left-hand side instead of the right. 

So, instead of:

```
library(tidyverse)
library(fs)

# current output formatting puts the ellipsis on the right side
x <- str_c("/lorem/ipsum/egestas/molestie/id/id/lacinia/feugiat/lacinia/augue/placerat/", c("apple", "banana", "cherry"), ".txt")
df <- tibble(path = fs::fs_path(x))
show(df)

# A tibble: 3 x 1
  path                                         
  <fs::path>                                   
1 /lorem/ipsum/egestas/molestie/id/id/lacinia/…
2 /lorem/ipsum/egestas/molestie/id/id/lacinia/…
3 /lorem/ipsum/egestas/molestie/id/id/lacinia/…
```

... one would instead (optionally) see something more like:

```
library(pillar)

# something like the desired output
df <- tibble(path = pillar::char(fs::fs_path(x), shorten = "front"))
show(df)

# A tibble: 3 x 1
  path                               
  <fs::path>                         
1 …/lacinia/augue/placerat/apple.txt 
2 …/lacinia/augue/placerat/banana.txt
3 …/lacinia/augue/placerat/cherry.txt
```

This could be useful when a long path prefix is common to all elements and the right side (the basenames and leaf-level subdirectories) is the thing that's varying a lot.

Maybe this could be controlled via `options(fs.fs_path.shorten = "front")`?

title: file_info does not fail or warn when file is missing
description:
I read in the [docs](https://fs.r-lib.org/reference/file_info.html) that `file_info` and `file_size` will fail if the file does not exist (or give a warning if `fail=FALSE`). However, it seems that the call does not fail, and instead returns `NA`. This is the same behavior as `file.size`.

Reprex:
``` r
library(fs)

file_size("this-file-does-not-exist", fail=TRUE)
#> NA
file_size("this-file-does-not-exist", fail=FALSE)
#> NA

```

I think this behavior is the function working as expected, at least according to the test below, but it does seem like the docs are out of date. https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/4cc4b56c26b9d7f177a676fbb331133bb2584b86/tests/testthat/test-file.R#L18-L25

title: dir_create() alters umask
description:
Example:

```R
Sys.umask()
#> [1] "22"
fs::dir_create('foo')
Sys.umask()
#> [1] "0"
```

Any files created after this point will be world readable and writable. For example:

```R
writeLines('abc', 'temp.txt')
file.mode('temp.txt')
#> [1] "666"
```

title: Permissions comparison not working as expected
description:
I'm hoping to check whether a file is private (i.e., has no group or other permissions granted). My approach has been to & those bits with "go+rwx" to highlight any group/other bits that are set and then check for equality with "go-rwx". This example, where I'm using `fs_perms("0640")` to represent a file with group read permissions, is returning `TRUE`, even though I'd expect the result to be `FALSE`:

```r
library(fs)

(fs_perms("0640") & fs_perms("g+rwx")) == "go-rwx"
```

Am I approaching the comparison operator incorrectly? I've tried several different ways to both set and compare the permissions.

title: Feature Request: `file_latest`
description:
It often need to identify the most version of a date-stamped file, such as `2020-08-21_analysis.R`, using the root, such as `analysis.R`. I currently use a separate `latest` function, but it would be great to have it integrated in `fs`.

I could imagine this function as `file_latest`, as well as perhaps `dir_latest` and `link_latest` similar to the `*_exists` functions but returning the file path.

Here's a how it might look:

``` r
# Project directory has a file called `2020-08-20_analysis.R`
dir_ls()
#> 2020-08-20_analysis.R

# Current function (returns boolean)

file_exists("analysis.R")
#> analysis.R
#> FALSE

file_exists("2020-08-20_analysis.R")
#> 2020-08-20_analysis.R
#> TRUE

# Suggested function (returns path)

file_latest("analysis.R")
#> 2020-08-20_analysis.R
#> 2020-08-20_analysis.R
```

Thank you for this package and for considering this feature request!

title: Add support for vctrs::vec_cast
description:
In many cases, it would be helpful to have the ability to cast integers, etc. to `fs_bytes`. For instance:

``` r
library(experiment)

vctrs::vec_cast(as.integer(c(2L, 4L)), fs::as_fs_bytes(1L))
#> Warning: The `vec_cast.fs_bytes` function is experimental and subject to change without warning in a future release
#> This warning is displayed once per session.
#> 2 4
```

<sup>Created on 2020-04-15 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

This required the following, and will require a `Suggests` dependency on `vctrs`:

```
#' @export
vec_cast.fs_bytes.integer <- function(x, to, ...) {
  warn_experimental("vec_cast.fs_bytes")
  fs::as_fs_bytes(x)
}

#' @export
vec_cast.fs_bytes.default <- function(x, to, ...) {
  vctrs::vec_default_cast(x = x, to = to)
}

#' @export
vec_cast.fs_bytes <- function(x, to, ...) {
  warn_experimental("vec_cast.fs_bytes")
  UseMethod("vec_cast.fs_bytes")
}


```

title: Recommended strategy for dealing with broken symlinks?
description:
Is there a recommended strategy for finding and gracefully handling broken symlinks? My package functions run `path_real()` on the project files to resolve any potential symlinks, and I had a user report a bug where a broken symlink broke everything. Is there a better option than always having to check with `is_link()`/`link_path()`/`file_exists()`?

Here is a reprex to demonstrate the issue:

``` r
packageVersion("fs")
#> [1] '1.3.1.9000'
library(fs)
d <- file_temp()
dir_create(d)
non_existent <- path(d, "non-existent")
broken_link <- path(d, "broken-link")
link_create(non_existent, broken_link)
file_exists(non_existent)
#> /tmp/RtmpeYDu12/file25f817354d04/non-existent 
#>                                         FALSE
link_exists(broken_link)
#> /tmp/RtmpeYDu12/file25f817354d04/broken-link 
#>                                         TRUE
link_path(broken_link)
#> /tmp/RtmpeYDu12/file25f817354d04/non-existent
file_exists(link_path(broken_link))
#> /tmp/RtmpeYDu12/file25f817354d04/non-existent 
#>                                         FALSE
f <- dir_ls(path = d)
path_real(f)
#> Error: [ENOENT] Failed to realize '/tmp/RtmpeYDu12/file25f817354d04/broken-link': no such file or directory
# Find any broken links
any(!file_exists(link_path(f[is_link(f)])))
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: Ability to resolve symlinks in file path when target file does not exist
description:
Would it be possible to add a feature to resolve symlinks in file paths even when the target file does not exist?

## Motivation

Often in my unit tests I use `tempfile()` to create temporary files. This creates a lot of headaches because on macOS only the file path returned contains a symlink (`/tmp -> private/tmp`). Thus the filepath returned by the function I am testing may or may not be the same as the one that it was passed depending on whether or not the function created the file. It would be convenient if a new or existing fs function had the ability to always resolve symlinks.

``` r
# Symlink not resolved when target file does not exist
f <- tempfile()
normalizePath(f, mustWork = FALSE)
#> [1] "/var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T//RtmpAEc0lL/fileab556f86b36"
fs::path_abs(f)
#> /var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T/RtmpAEc0lL/fileab556f86b36
# fs::path_real(f) throws error

# Symlink is resolved when target file exists
file.create(f)
#> [1] TRUE
normalizePath(f)
#> [1] "/private/var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T/RtmpAEc0lL/fileab556f86b36"
fs::path_abs(f)
#> /var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T/RtmpAEc0lL/fileab556f86b36
fs::path_real(f)
#> /private/var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T/RtmpAEc0lL/fileab556f86b36
```

<sup>Created on 2018-10-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1.9000)</sup>

## Proof of concept

I wrote the following function `resolve_symlink()` as a current solution.

``` r
# Resolve symlinks in a filepath even if file does not exist.
#
# Input: Vector of absolute filepaths
# Output: Vector of absolute filepaths with any symlinks resolved
resolve_symlink <- function(path) {
  return(vapply(path, resolve_symlink_, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE))
}

# Recursive function to resolve symlinks one path at a time.
resolve_symlink_ <- function(path) {
  # Base case #1: If path exists, resolve symlink
  if (fs::file_exists(path)) {
    return(fs::path_real(path))
  }

  parts <- fs::path_split(path)[[1]]
  len <- length(parts)

  # Base case #2: Only 1 part of file path remaining. Return it.
  #
  # Possible cases:
  #   * Invalid input such as NA
  #   * A Fake file path that doesn't exist on the machine
  if (len == 1) {
    return(path)
  }

  # Recursive case
  return(fs::path_join(c(
    resolve_symlink(fs::path_join(parts[-len])),
    parts[len])))
}

f <- tempfile()
normalizePath(f, mustWork = FALSE)
#> [1] "/var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T//RtmpPB54b2/file16f543497332"
fs::path_abs(f)
#> /var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T/RtmpPB54b2/file16f543497332
resolve_symlink(f)
#> [1] "/private/var/folders/5b/hbjnbkkd0t957rs24vxgvw200000gn/T/RtmpPB54b2/file16f543497332"
```

title: `dir_delete` fails when `path` contains nested directories.
description:
If the `path` argument to `dir_delete` contains nested subdirectories, `dir_delete` will delete the subdirectories, but will fail prior to deleting the top level directories:

```
test <- c("~/test/about", "~/test/tags",  "~/test/tags/blogdown")
dir_create(test)  # Make sure there is no existing ~/test directory first.
dir_ls("~/test", recurse = TRUE) %>% as.character()
## [1] "/home/michael/test/about"         "/home/michael/test/tags"         
## [3] "/home/michael/test/tags/blogdown"
dir_delete(test)
## Error: [ENOENT] Failed to remove '/home/michael/test/tags/blogdown': no such file or directory
dir_ls("~/test", recurse = TRUE) %>% as.character()
## [1] "/home/michael/test/about" "/home/michael/test/tags" 
```

This happens because `dir_delete` itself goes off and gets subdirectories to delete, and then concatenates them with the original top-level directories before deleting:

```
old <- path_expand(path)
dirs <- dir_ls(old, type = "directory", recurse = TRUE, 
  all = TRUE)
# ...
rmdir_(rev(c(old, dirs)))
```

If `path` had subdirectories in it, `c(old, dirs)` will include subdirectories twice, so it fails the second time it gets to one.

A solution would be to wrap `c(old, dirs)` in `unique`:

```
rmdir_(rev(unique(c(old, dirs), fromLast = TRUE)))
```

This works in my testing. Happy to (try to) create a pull request if appropriate.

Versions:
fs 1.3.1
R 3.6.1
RStudio 1.2.5019

title: Feature request: dir_ls() family - argument to ignore temporary MS Office files
description:
All below is for OS X.

MS Office has an awful habit of creating a temporary file for any open files in the same directory, ie "myfile.xlsx" when opened creates a temporary file "~$myfile.xlsx".  Thus using a "*.xlsx" grob captures these.

Unfortunately, `all = F` to not return hidden files does not seem to apply to these files. 

Of course you can use `regexp` to filter these, but since the files only appear when another file is open, it's very easy to not catch that it's necessary if writing code without any files open that then pop up later if someone is looking at one of the files they are about to read in (fairly common in my experience).  In addition, the `regexp` argument wont' work along side the `grob` argument.

Perhaps the `all` argument could be updated to include filtering things that start with "~$"?  Or a new arg to ignore temporary MS Office files could be added with the default set to TRUE?

title: dir_ls() with regexp is inconsistent with list.files()
description:
Hi,

This might be a design choice, and is a matter of adjusting my code, and centers around the `^` start-of-line marker in the `regexp` argument. Somewhat related to https://github.com/r-lib/fs/issues/127.

`list.files(path, pattern = '^abc', recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)` seems to first get all the files, then apply the pattern to filter, and then prepend the full path. `dir_ls()` first gets the full list of files, incl. full path, and then filters using `path_filter()`. 

The net effect is that the `^abc` pattern from `list.files()` does not work (or needs to be converted to something, possibly, more complicated to achieve the same effect). Given that the function comparison vignette "equates" `dir_ls()` with `list.files()` I would expect them to behave more similar regarding the filtering *or* to be more clearly documented to be different (it is somewhere to be read between the lines of the second bullet of that comparison vignette, but only vaguely).

title: Unknown type name 'uuid_t'
Should `[[` preserve class
description:
It looks like the fs methods for `[[` strip the class:

```r
fs_path(c("foo", "bar"))[1]
#> foo

fs_path(c("foo", "bar"))[[1]]
#> [1] "foo"
```

I think the class of atomic vectors should be preserved by `[[`, the only effect should be to strip vectorised attributes like names.

One concrete problem caused by this behaviour is that these vectors can't be spliced correctly (with dev rlang and @DavisVaughan's patch, CRAN rlang still uses `as.list()`):

```r
rlang::list2(!!!fs_path(c("foo", "bar")))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "foo"
#>
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "bar"
```

Same for `purrr::map()` which uses `[[`

```r
purrr::map(fs_path(c("foo", "bar")), identity)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "foo"
#>
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "bar"
```

And same for a future `vctrs::vec_chop2()` (which would be aliased to `vec_as_list()`).

title: path_has_parent() documentation doesn't communicate that it's a predicate
description:
When I tried to use `path_has_parent()`, I assumed it would look at each element of `path` to see if `parent` was the element's parent. I expected this:
```
> fs::path_has_parent(path = c("/a/b/c", "/x/y/z"), parent = "/a/b")
[1]  TRUE FALSE
```
but instead I got `FALSE`.

Generally, I thought it would  work like this:
```
path_has_parent <- function(path, parent) {
  purrr::map_lgl(path, ~fs::path_common(c(.x, parent)) == parent)
}
```

Obviously, this function can do whatever the author wants it to do, but the documentation doesn't communicate what it does. There aren't any examples, either; there's just one line in the **Functions** section of `?fs::path_math`:
> **`path_has_parent`**: determine if a path has a given parent.

Since the [top advertised advantage of the `fs` functions over base functions](https://github.com/r-lib/fs) is that `fs` functions are vectorized, I think that this `fs` predicate function needs more documentation.

title: Better supported for organised subdirectory structures
description:
Often, one has an organised directory structure e.g. of the format `/<country>/<year>` and then needs to do some batch processing of files in these directories. A typical workflow would be to get info about a certain file in each of these directories and parse parts of the path to the file, e.g.

``` r
library(fs)
library(dplyr)
dir_info("~/Downloads/", recurse = TRUE, regexp = "(es|de|fr)/\\d{4}/population\\.xlsx") %>% 
  transmute(
    country = stringr::str_match(path, "(es|de|fr)/(\\d{4})/population\\.xlsx")[, 2],
    year = stringr::str_match(path, "(es|de|fr)/(\\d{4})/population\\.xlsx")[, 3],
    size
  )
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   country year         size
#>   <chr>   <chr> <fs::bytes>
#> 1 de      2000        2.95M
#> 2 de      2001        2.95M
#> 3 de      2002        2.95M
#> 4 fr      2000        2.95M
#> 5 fr      2002        2.95M
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

and then process each file passing path, country and year as a parameter to the corresponding function.

Instead of the code above it would be very nice to have something like

``` r
dir_info("~/Downloads/", parts = c(country = "es|de|fr", year = "\\d{4}", "population\\.rds"))
```

i.e. specify the parts of the path and the named parts should become a column in the output.

Further, it would make sense to also support this in `dir_map()` and `dir_walk()` and pass the parsed parts of the path on to fun, i.e.

``` r
dir_walk(
  "~/Downloads/",
  parts = c(country = "es|de|fr", year = "\\d{4}", "population\\.rds"),
  fun = function(path, country, year) {}
)
```

title: dir_exists(".") returns TRUE when current working directory is deleted
description:
I found an edge case where both `dir.exists(".")` and `fs::dir_exists(".")` return `TRUE` when the current working directory has been deleted. 

I'd like to be able to write code similar to below. It converts a relative path to a directory to an absolute path.

```
if (fs::dir_exists(relative_path_to_directory) {
  absolute_path_to_directory <- fs::path_abs(relative_path_to_directory)
}
```

The above code fails in this edge case when `path_abs()` tries to convert the relative path to the non-existent current working directory.

Is it possible to update `fs::dir_exists()` to handle this edge case? If not, what is the best way to handle it in my code? I also tried `fs::is_dir()` but it also returns `TRUE`.

Here's a reprex to demonstrate this behavior with both base R and fs functions:

``` r

cwd <- getwd()
path <- tempfile()
dir.create(path)
setwd(path)
unlink(path, recursive = TRUE, force = TRUE)
dir.exists(path)
#> [1] FALSE
dir.exists(".")
#> [1] TRUE
getwd()
#> NULL
setwd(cwd)

cwd <- fs::path_wd()
path <- fs::file_temp()
fs::dir_create(path)
setwd(path)
fs::dir_delete(path)
fs::dir_exists(path)
#> /tmp/RtmpP3SGE9/file3ca72edbcba1 
#>                            FALSE
fs::dir_exists(".")
#>    . 
#> TRUE
fs::is_dir(".")
#>    . 
#> TRUE
if (dir.exists(".")) fs::path_abs(".")
#> Error in path[!is_abs] <- path_norm(path(start, path[!is_abs])): replacement has length zero
fs::path_wd()
#> character(0)
setwd(cwd)

title: link_delete is broken in dev version 1.3.1.9000
description:
My package's unit tests fail with the development version of fs. I investigated, and the problem appears to be with the function `link_delete()`.

With fs 1.3.1, the code below runs fine:

``` r

packageVersion("fs")
#> [1] '1.3.1'
d <- fs::file_temp()
fs::dir_create(d)
l <- fs::file_temp()
fs::link_create(d, l)
identical(fs::link_path(l), d)
#> [1] TRUE
fs::dir_exists(d)
#> /tmp/RtmpnnlI3x/file2e1a39e50243 
#>                             TRUE
fs::link_exists(l)
#> /tmp/RtmpnnlI3x/file2e1a19a04231 
#>                             TRUE
fs::link_delete(l)
fs::dir_exists(d)
#> /tmp/RtmpnnlI3x/file2e1a39e50243 
#>                             TRUE
fs::link_exists(l)
#> /tmp/RtmpnnlI3x/file2e1a19a04231 
#>                            FALSE
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-21 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9000)</sup>


However, with the development version 1.3.1.9000, `link_delete()` fails to delete the link:

``` r

packageVersion("fs")
#> [1] '1.3.1.9000'
d <- fs::file_temp()
fs::dir_create(d)
l <- fs::file_temp()
fs::link_create(d, l)
identical(fs::link_path(l), d)
#> [1] TRUE
fs::dir_exists(d)
#> /tmp/RtmpKU2BG2/file1cee499ea170 
#>                             TRUE
fs::link_exists(l)
#> /tmp/RtmpKU2BG2/file1cee2ab33ed8 
#>                             TRUE
fs::link_delete(l)
#> Error: [ENOTDIR] Failed to remove '/tmp/RtmpKU2BG2/file1cee2ab33ed8': not a directory
fs::dir_exists(d)
#> /tmp/RtmpKU2BG2/file1cee499ea170 
#>                             TRUE
fs::link_exists(l)
#> /tmp/RtmpKU2BG2/file1cee2ab33ed8 
#>                             TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-21 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9000)</sup>

I ran the code above on Ubuntu 18.04. Please let me know if you'd like me to run it on other operating systems.

title: No (direct) fs equivalent for base::file.mtime()
description:
While you can pull the `modification_time` column from `fs::file_info()`, there is no {fs} equivalent for `base::file.mtime()`.

``` r
pacman::p_load(fs, dplyr)

# create files
dir_create("/tmp/test")
file_create("/tmp/test/temp1.txt")
Sys.sleep(60)
file_create("/tmp/test/temp2.txt")

# using fs and dplyr
dir_ls("/tmp/test") %>% 
  file_info() %>% 
  pull(modification_time)
#> [1] "2019-07-16 15:59:44 EDT" "2019-07-16 16:00:44 EDT"

# using base
file.mtime(list.files("/tmp/test", full.names = TRUE))
#> [1] "2019-07-16 15:59:44 EDT" "2019-07-16 16:00:44 EDT"
```

title: Convenience functions to check file permissions
description:
It would be convenient to have functions that return TRUE/FALSE depending on the file permissions, e.g. `file_is_readable()`, `file_is_writeable()`, and `file_is_executable()`. Checking for different users could be done with arguments, e.g. `file_is_readable("file.txt", user = TRUE, group = TRUE, other = FALSE)`.

In the short term, I appreciate that I can get this information by parsing `fs::file_info()$permissions`. Below is the simple prototype I am using for now.

```
file_is_executable <- function(f) {
  stopifnot(fs::file_exists(f))
  perms <- fs::file_info(f)$permissions
  perms <- as.character(perms)
  perms <- stringr::str_split_fixed(perms, "", n = 9)
  perms <- as.character(perms)
  if (perms[3] == "x" || perms[6] == "x" || perms[9] == "x") {
    return(TRUE)
  }
  return(FALSE)
}
```

Related question. How can I reliably get the octal format as a number from an `fs_perms` object? My first idea for to determining if a file was executable or not was to check the octal representation for odd numbers.

If I passed the octal representation to `fs_perms()`, then I was able to retrieve it:

```
perms <- fs::fs_perms("644")
class(perms)
## [1] "fs_perms" "integer" 
as.numeric(as.character(as.octmode(perms)))
## [1] 644
```

However, I get a different result if the permissions are created by `file_info()`:

```
f <- fs::file_temp()
fs::file_create(f)
perms <- fs::file_info(f)$permissions
class(perms)
## [1] "fs_perms"
perms
## [1] rw-r--r--
as.numeric(as.character(as.octmode(perms)))
## [1] 100644
```

Shouldn't these be the same since the file was also "644"?
