title: Behaviour when copying a file onto itself
description: I wonder if `fs::file_copy()` should behave like `cp` here, which refuses to copy a file onto itself, even with `-f`? --- A study of copying a file onto itself, in R vs. the shell. Motivated by this troubleshooting in rcmdcheck: https://github.com/r-lib/rcmdcheck/pull/86 https://github.com/r-lib/rcmdcheck/issues/87 fs complains about copying to a pre-existing file. With `overwrite = TRUE`, it seems to silently unlink it and write a new file with requested name but no content. library(fs) writeLines("I have content!", "~/tmp/foo.txt") readLines("~/tmp/foo.txt") #> [1] "I have content!" file_copy("~/tmp/foo.txt", "~/tmp") #> Error: [EEXIST] Failed to copy '/Users/jenny/tmp/foo.txt' to '/Users/jenny/tmp/foo.txt': file already exists file_copy("~/tmp/foo.txt", "~/tmp", overwrite = TRUE) readLines("~/tmp/foo.txt") #> character(0) Base R effectively does same, but with more mystifying communications. writeLines("I have content!", "~/tmp/foo.txt") file.copy("~/tmp/foo.txt", "~/tmp") #> [1] FALSE readLines("~/tmp/foo.txt") #> [1] "I have content!" file.copy("~/tmp/foo.txt", "~/tmp", overwrite = TRUE) #> [1] TRUE readLines("~/tmp/foo.txt") #> character(0) `cp` in the shell cannot even be forced to overwrite a file with itself. Note that it always errors about the target file being identical to the source file. echo 'I have content!' > ~/tmp/foo.txt cat ~/tmp/foo.txt cp ~/tmp/foo.txt ~/tmp cp -f ~/tmp/foo.txt ~/tmp cat ~/tmp/foo.txt #> I have content! #> cp: /Users/jenny/tmp/foo.txt and /Users/jenny/tmp/foo.txt are identical (not copied). #> cp: /Users/jenny/tmp/foo.txt and /Users/jenny/tmp/foo.txt are identical (not copied). #> I have content!

title: ENOENT error with dir_ls() when hidden file is in path
description:
Under Windows 10, some directories can only be accessed by an administrator. Where R doesn't have enough permission to see a directory, the behavior of `fs::dir_ls()` and `dir()` differs: `dir_ls()` throws an error, but `dir()` silently ignores the existence of that directory.

For example, when searching the Program Files directory, I see

``` r
library(fs)
program_files <- "%ProgramFiles%"
dir_ls(program_files)
#> Error: [ENOENT] Failed to search directory '%ProgramFiles%': no such file or directory
dir(program_files)
#> character(0)
```

This behavior of `dir_ls()` seems fine in the non-recursive case. However, when `recursive = TRUE`, it seems preferable to skip directories where there is not enough permission.

I'm struggling to create a completely reproducible example, but here's the motivating example that led me to find this. I tried recursively searching `~`. Kaspersky Password Manager is installed, and this stores some data in an admin-protected folder inside the `%LocalAppData%` directory, which is  a subdirectory of `~`. I ran this while logged in as under a Windows admin account.

``` r
library(fs)
dir_ls("~", recursive = TRUE)
#> Error: [EPERM] Failed to search directory 'C:/Users/richie/AppData/Local/Kaspersky Lab/Kaspersky Password Manager': operation not permitted
```

Here's the traceback.

```
4: (function (..., call. = TRUE, domain = NULL) 
   {
       args <- list(...)
       if (length(args) == 1L && inherits(args[[1L]], "condition")) {
           cond <- args[[1L]]
           if (nargs() > 1L) 
               warning("additional arguments ignored in stop()")
           message <- conditionMessage(cond)
           call <- conditionCall(cond)
           .Internal(.signalCondition(cond, message, call))
           .Internal(.dfltStop(message, call))
       }
       else .Internal(stop(call., .makeMessage(..., domain = domain)))
   })(list(message = "[EPERM] Failed to search directory 'C:/Users/richie/AppData/Local/Kaspersky Lab/Kaspersky Password Manager': operation not permitted"))
3: dir_map_(old, fun, all, sum(directory_entry_types[type]), recursive, 
       fail)
2: dir_map(old, identity, all, recursive, type, fail)
1: dir_ls("~", recursive = TRUE)
```


The problem seems to be that the list of directories to search is created with high enough permission to see that the Kaspersky directory exists, then some operation is applied with lower permission that throws an error when it tries to access that directory.

This means that the user doesn't get to see the contents of any of the directories that they do have permission to access.

I think it makes sense to follow the behavior of `dir()` in the recursive case, and just ignore the contents of any subdirectories that the user doesn't have permission to see. Throwing a warning rather than an error would also be an option.

title: Installation error
Comparison table: base R vs fs
fs does not compile on openbsd
description:
Installing "tidyverse" in R op openbsd 6.4 ( on 6.3 it works) throws errors because fs (and likely consequently reprex) wont compile; on r/openbsd I asked if anyone experienced that also; which was confirmed by u/vtail57; he dug into it and came up with an offending line:
https://github.com/r-lib/fs/blob/73bde0d42fce4acc786f4610e81ca2ede4d32f49/src/unix/getmode.cc#L3

#if (defined(__APPLE__) && defined(__MACH__)) || defined(__BSD__)

running: cpp -dM /dev/null | grep -i BSD shows that only __OpenBSD__ is defined by clang 6.0.0, which is a C compiler shipping with OpenBSD 6.4.

This my first reporting issue ever so if it not complies to the proper guidelines apologies

```r
  if (is.character(group_id)) {
    group_id<- getgrnam_(group_id)
}
```

I'll do a PR with a test

title: Add vectorized `path_join` with multiple parameters
description:
Use case:

I have a list of files, a directory, and want a fully qualified path to the files. I could perhaps work around this with `path_rel` with a different start point (or `paste`), but I think having a way to easily concatenate the files together with some type of `path_join` would be nice.

``` r
# I have a handful of files
files <- c("one", "two", "three")
files_list <- list("one", "two", "three")

# in a directory
current_dir <- "./path/to/files"

# i want the full path to these files
fs::path_join(list(current_dir, files))
#> ./path/to/files one/two/three
fs::path_join(c(current_dir, files))
#> ./path/to/files/one/two/three
fs::path_join(list(current_dir, files_list))
#> Error in vapply(parts, path_join, character(1)): values must be length 1,
#>  but FUN(X[[2]]) result is length 3
fs::path_join(c(current_dir, files_list))
#> ./path/to/files one             two             three

# ideally... something like
# fs::path_join(current_dir, files)
#> ./path/to/files/one ./path/to/files/two ./path/to/files/three
#>

# workaround
paste(current_dir, files, sep = "/")
#> [1] "./path/to/files/one"   "./path/to/files/two"   "./path/to/files/three"
```

package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

title: file_temp() handles extensions differently
description:
`file_temp()` passes it's arguments to `tempfile()` so the dot before the extension isn't added when `ext` is supplied.

``` r
fs::file_temp(ext = "png")
#> /var/folders/zw/8z2vpz1s0cl3gwpyh5p72mwh0000gn/T/RtmpCH0bFk/file182f41b49023bpng
```

But all other functions in `fs` do add the dot.

``` r
fs::path("image", ext = "png")
#> image.png
fs::path_wd("image", ext = "png")
#> /private/var/folders/zw/8z2vpz1s0cl3gwpyh5p72mwh0000gn/T/RtmpK6r2gf/reprex1539e7ebfaa4/image.png
fs::path_ext_set("image", ext = "png")
#> image.png
```

They all have similar documentation

    path(..., ext = "")
    path_wd(..., ext = "")
        ext An optional extension to append to the generated path.
    
    path_ext_set(path, ext)
    path_ext(path) <- value
        ext, value The new file extension.
        
    file_temp(pattern = "file", tmp_dir = tempdir(), ext = "")
        ext The file extension of the temporary file.

so it's easy to miss this detail. The examples for `file_temp()` mention that its arguments are passed on to `tempfile()`, but I think it’s easy to overlook the implication that the `.` is required (especially because this information doesn't appear in the RStudio autocomplete helper).

``` r
tempfile(fileext = "png")
#> [1] "/var/folders/zw/8z2vpz1s0cl3gwpyh5p72mwh0000gn/T//RtmpCH0bFk/file182f47b2d70e8png"
```

It would be nice to to mention this difference in the documentation of `ext` in `file_temp()`, or even better for `ext` to behave similarly across `fs`.
<sup>Created on 2018-10-06 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

title: globs and file paths?
description:
I'm trying to emulate the common `ls` behavior with globs and file paths.  I thought that the `path` argument would effectively be the  "working directory" for `ls` call and that the glob could include paths, but this doesn't seem to be the case, e.g.

```r
fs::dir_create("data/stuff")
fs::dir_create("data/stuff2")
fs::file_create("data/stuff/good.tsv")
fs::dir_ls(glob = "data/*/*.tsv")
```
does not find `good.tsv`, but running `ls data/*/*.tsv` from the terminal with the same working dir (`.`) does.  If the path part doesn't have wild-cards I can manually split this into a path and a final glob, and include whatever base working directory, e.g. something like:

```r
proj_dir  ="."
g = "data/*/*.tsv"

path <- fs::path_join(c(proj_dir, fs::path_rel(fs::path_dir(g))))
glob <- fs::path_file(g)
fs::dir_ls(path = path, glob = glob, recursive = TRUE)
```

but this won't work for the example above where the path includes a glob.  (Context: I'd like to reliably parse files like .gitattributes to identify all files "tracked" by git lfs).

title: `move_file` deletes files when `new_path` contains duplicates: Fail would be preferable.
description:
The description of `file_move()` says that it always fails if it is unable to move a file. This gives the impression that it is a safer version of `file.rename()`.

However, when you pass a character vector containing duplicates as `new_path`, it silently deletes files. To really be a safe function, `file_move()` should check wheter `new_path` contains duplicates. If so, if should fail.

title: fs::dir_ls("C:") returns Error: [EBUSY] Failed to stat 'C:/hiberfil.sys': resource busy or locked
description:

Windows causes some problems. e.g., directories with non-latin characters (e.g., папка) are translated fo "?????" which is not great (see example below). It seems `fs` can deal with these types of issues *much* better but I'm hitting some snags there as well. `list.files("C:")` has only one problems (note the ???? directory) but `fs::dir_ls("C:")` only returns an error.

Is there a work around you can suggest @jimhester? Thanks.


title: Error: `m` must be a match object from `regexpr()` when using path_ext on filename with non-latin characters
Function to detect if path A is "in" path B
description:
Came up in the fs-ification of usethis.

Something along these lines, but more general (my path B is hard-wired to `proj_get()`, which is guaranteed to be realized):

``` r
is_in_proj <- function(path) {
  ## realize path, if possible; use "as is", otherwise
  path <- tryCatch(path_real(path), error = function(e) NULL) %||% path
  identical(
    proj_get(),
    path_common(c(proj_get(), path))
  )
}
```

title: Preservation of double slashes in, e.g., "https://"
description:
I've been in the habit of using `file.path()` and, therefore, potentially `fs::path()` to make URLs, when the URL-building tools in httr would be overkill.

``` r
fs::path("https://github.com/tidyverse/principles", "issues", "4")
#> https:/github.com/tidyverse/principles/issues/4
```

But fs turns the double slash in "https://" to a single slash, breaking the URL. Should that (and similar protocols) be special-cased?

title: Should dir_create() etc take ...?
description: And pass onto `path()` for you.

title: Improve documentation for path
description: Multiple people have not realized `fs::path()` is the fs, equivalent of `file.path()`, we should make this more clear in examples / README.

title: Emulate behaviour of cp when target is directory
description:
Any interest in emulating this aspect of cp (second line) in `file_copy()`?

```
cp [-R [-H | -L | -P]] [-fi | -n] [-apvX] source_file target_file
cp [-R [-H | -L | -P]] [-fi | -n] [-apvX] source_file ... target_directory
```

``` r
library(fs)

source_file <- path(R.home("doc"), "THANKS")
target_directory <- dir_create("just_hold_me")
file_copy(source_file, target_directory)
#> Error: [EEXIST] Failed to copy '/Library/Frameworks/R.framework/Resources/doc/THANKS' to 'just_hold_me': file already exists

file_copy(source_file, path(target_directory, path_file(source_file)))
dir_ls(target_directory)
#> just_hold_me/THANKS
```

Created on 2018-04-19 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

What if the first call to `file_copy()` "just worked", i.e. gave the result from the second call? We basically did this in googledrive and it seems nice. But I also had/have some misgivings that it's too helpful.

title: Feature Suggestion: resolve "~" to "%UserProfile%"
description: In OSX, "~" is a path shortcut to the user home directory.  It is useful to get around paths that differ depending on what user is logged in.  Would be great if it would work for PC's too to make paths cross-platform by resolving to %UserProfile%.

title: Question: fs::path() usage for xxxx:// type paths
description:
I typically use `fs` for any path related operations, which was fine when I worked on my local machine. I've recently started writing code to be deployed in an Azure environment. I have to store files in the blob storage and have a path like:

`mainpath <- "wasb://manymanyletters@abce.blob.core.windows.net/foldername"`

As a result running

`output_path <- fs::path(mainpath, 'out')`

results in

`wasb:/manymanyletters@abce.blob.core.windows.net/foldername/out`

Notice the single `/` after `wasb:`.

Is there a different function or workaround to generate paths with `wasb://` or `https://` using the `fs` package?

title: Misleading ENOENT when attempting to `file_copy` to the same location twice
description:
If you try to `file_copy` a single file with `overwrite = FALSE` and the destination`new_path` already exists, you get a `EEXIST` error. `file_copy` is vectorized, and if you have any duplicates in `new_path`, you might expect to get the same error: the first copy would succeed, and the second one would fail with "file already exists". Instead, you get an incorrect "no such file or directory" (`ENOENT`) error, which points you in the wrong direction for debugging your code.

This test:

```
test_that("file_copy errors usefully", {
  tmp <- tempfile()
  dir_create(tmp)
  cat("", file=file.path(tmp, "a.txt"))
  
  expect_error(
    file_copy(rep(file.path(tmp, "a.txt"), 2), rep(file.path(tmp, "b.txt"), 2)),
    "EEXIST"
  )
})
```

fails like this: 

```
`file_copy(...)` threw an error with unexpected message.
Expected match: "EEXIST"
Actual message: "[ENOENT] Failed to copy '/var/folders/ly/dnxts6pd22q98109b0nsbq2h0000gp/T/RtmpvSTXbY/fileb73b130ed4bb/a.txt' to '/var/folders/ly/dnxts6pd22q98109b0nsbq2h0000gp/T/RtmpvSTXbY/fileb73b130ed4bb/b.txt': no such file or directory"
```

title: Class of returned object for path_tidy/new_fs_path
description:
Hey,

I was recently trying to switch my workflow from base functions to fs functions, and it works quite well, however some functions will fail when the value of fs function is given to them since they do not use method for the fs_path class. Here is an example where I store intermediate files as temporary ones in a raster workflow.

```
tempfile_base <- tempfile(fileext = ".tif") 
class(tempfile_base)
[1] "character"
tempfile_fs <- fs::file_temp(ext = ".tif") 
class(tempfile_fs)
[1] "fs_path"   "character"

r <- raster::raster(volcano)
raster::writeRaster(r, tempfile_base) # Works fine
raster::writeRaster(r, tempfile_fs)
# > Error in (function (classes, fdef, mtable)  :
  unable to find an inherited method for function ‘writeRaster’ for signature ‘"RasterLayer", "fs_path"’
```

I'm not sure if this is an actual issue or not, since it is easily solved by wrapping it in as.character() function, so this is more like a feedback for the package API. I assume that there is a good reason for having the returned value as fs_path class (colors/encoding?!?), maybe a solution would be to have return as.character argument (would this break the consistency in returning the UTF path?!?).

Cheers and thanks for the work on this package!

title: `link_create` cannot create soft file symbol link on Windows
description:
Thank you guys for this amazing package.

I found that `fs::link_create` could not create ***soft*** file symbol link on Windows but only soft directory symbol link. However `base::file.symlink` could:

```r
library(fs)

dir <- dir_create("dir")
file <- file_create(path(dir, "file.txt"))

link_create(path_abs(dir), path_abs("dir_link"))
link_create(path_abs(file), path_abs("file_link"))
file.symlink(path_abs(file), path_abs("file_link_base_r"))
```

```powershell
## In powershell
> ls

## Mode                LastWriteTime         Length Name                                                                         
## ----                -------------         ------ ----

## d----l         2018/3/3      0:32                file_link
```

Is there any way to create soft file symbol link using `fs` package?

title: Have `file_delete()` handle directories as well
Vectorize `file_chmod`?
description:
Any plan on vectorizing `file_chmod`? Below is a comparison of `file_chmod()` and `Sys.chmod`:

```R
library(tidyverse)
library(fs)
packageVersion("fs")
#> [1] '1.1.0.9000'
```

#### Create two test files

```R
x <- file_create(file_temp(), "000") 
x
#> /var/folders/m8/68z5d14d7mv9qyf1bd69ych40000gn/T/RtmpOedRyI/file10e2c4e590608
file_info(x) %>% select(permissions)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   permissions
#>   <fs::perms>
#> 1 ---------

y <- file_create(file_temp(), "444")
y
#> /var/folders/m8/68z5d14d7mv9qyf1bd69ych40000gn/T/RtmpOedRyI/file10e2c369b1f67
file_info(y) %>% select(permissions)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   permissions
#>   <fs::perms>
#> 1 r--r--r--
```

#### `Sys.chmod()` can set permissions of one or more files

```R
Sys.chmod(c(x, y), "777", use_umask = FALSE)
file_info(x) %>% select(permissions)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   permissions
#>   <fs::perms>
#> 1 rwxrwxrwx
file_info(y) %>% select(permissions)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   permissions
#>   <fs::perms>
#> 1 rwxrwxrwx
```

#### `file_chmod()` can't handle more than one file

```R
file_chmod(c(x, y), "666")
#> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...): Expecting a single value: [extent=2].
```

If it's an intended feature, perhaps it'd help to add an example for handling multiple files? Something like

```R
x <- file_create(file_temp(), "000") 
y <- file_create(file_temp(), "444")
lapply(c(x, y), file_chmod, mode = "777")
file_info(x)$permissions
file_info(y)$permissions
```

title: Windows home directory
description:
On Windows, R sets the `R_USER` environment variable to the user's `Documents` folder, and R uses this as the 'home' directory (for e.g. tilde-path expansion). This implies that by default:

```R
> path.expand("~")
[1] "C:/Users/kevin/Documents"
> fs::path_home()
C:/Users/kevin/Documents
> Sys.getenv("R_USER")
[1] "C:/Users/kevin/Documents"
```

This seems a bit counter-intuitive as this folder is not really the user's "home" directory. The associated logic R uses to choose this path is here and below:

https://github.com/wch/r-source/blob/9bec1ec8b544e077cbb35f190ad9c62a99876190/src/gnuwin32/shext.c#L26-L45

Would it make sense for `fs` to enforce the 'real' home directory (as set with e.g. `%USERPROFILE%` or `%HOMEDRIVE%%HOMEPATH%`)?

title: How to handle missing values?
description:
Following up on #63, the functions vary in how they handle missing values. Some return `NA`, some return `FALSE`, and others throw an error.

## Proposal

I propose the following functionality for handling missing values:

* `path_*` functions return `NA`
* `is_*` functions return `FALSE`
* All other functions throw an error

## Current status

Here is the current status of fs functions:

* Return `NA`: path_abs, path_ext_remove, path_filter, path_norm, path_split, path_tidy
* Return `FALSE`: is_absolute_path
* Throw error: dir_copy, dir_create, dir_delete, dir_exists, dir_info, dir_ls, dir_map, dir_walk, file_access, file_chmod, file_chown, file_copy, file_create, file_delete, file_exists, file_info, file_move, file_show, file_temp_push, is_dir, is_file, is_link, link_copy, link_create, link_delete, link_exists, link_path, path_common, path_dir, path_expand, path_ext, path_ext_set, path_ext<-, path_file, path_real, path_rel

Here is the code I used to generate these lists:

```
library("fs")
funs <- ls(name = "package:fs")
result <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(funs))
names(result) <- funs
for (i in seq_along(funs)) {
  exec <- get(funs[i])
  arguments <- names(formals(exec))
  if (length(arguments) > 0 && arguments[1] == "path") {
    result[[i]] <- tryCatch(exec(NA), error = function(e) "error")
  } else {
    result[[i]] <- "No path argument"
  }
}
# Return NA
cat(names(result)[sapply(result, is.na)], sep = ", ")
# Return FALSE
cat(names(result)[sapply(result, function(x) x == "FALSE" && !is.na(x))], sep = ", ")
# Throw error
cat(names(result)[sapply(result, function(x) x == "error" && !is.na(x))], sep = ", ")
```

title: `path()` silently ignores zero-length input
description:
This is probably just a matter of taste, but `path()` behaves differently compared to `file.path()` for 0-length input:
```r
file.path("a", character(0)) # -> character(0)
fs::path("a", character(0)) # -> "a"
```
If the second part is the result of some kind of filtering (`is_dir()`, `file.mtime()`, ...), you might end up accidentally deleting the base directory instead of only those candidates for which the filter criterion holds (which is exactly how I stumbled about this).

title: file hash
description:
Would it be worthwhile to have a file hash as a column in `file_info()`? I often want to be able to compare either different versions of the same filename or different filenames but the same file.

This could be as simple as 

```
res$hash <- tools::md5sum(path)
```

or via some other mechanism.

title: `dir_copy` removes files in target directory
description:
```r
dir_create(c("a", "b"))
file_create(path("a", "foo"))
file_create(path("b", "bar"))
dir_copy("a", "b", overwrite = TRUE)
dir_ls("b") # file bar is deleted
```

I don't know if this is intended, but it is not clearly documented and could lead to unwanted data loss. :worried:

title: alternate permission / attribute input / output on windows
description:
Windows does not really have analogous permissions to POSIX systems, all you can really change is write permissions (whether the file is read-only or not). Also the concept of hidden files as an attribute is different than POSIX. Therefore it might make sense to have a different class than `fs_perms` on windows to display the attributes as `Get-ChildItem` does.

https://stackoverflow.com/a/4940052/2055486 has explanations of the format.

title: Clarify file_move vs. file_rename
description:
```R
file_move("x.txt", "y")
file_rename("x.txt", "y.txt")
```

`file_rename(x, y)` must have `length(x) == length(y)`, where in `file_move()` `length(y)` could also be one (if you want to move many files into the same directory)

`file_rename()` needs `overwrite` argument, to check if any files exist (and are not directories). `file_move()` needs to check that the RHS is a directory.
